query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The wear resistance and microscopic deformation of a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating on a conventional metal substrate during sliding in the high-temperature operating regime are governed by the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) and the alloy's intrinsic structure sensitivity to tribochemical reactions.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating on a conventional metal substrate
generation.intervention: Introduction of oxidation-prone alloying elements into the alloy matrix
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved wear resistance and reduced microscopic deformation
generation.baseline: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating without oxidation-prone alloying elements
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition and microstructure of the alloy, as well as the specific tribochemical reactions involved

falsification_experiment.design: Sliding wear test at high temperature (700 °C) with varying alloy compositions and microstructures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of oxidation-prone alloying elements does not lead to improved wear resistance and reduced microscopic deformation, the hypothesis is falsified.

Tribo-oxidation may promote the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication [,,]. If the worn surface is replaced by a glaze layer as tribo-oxidation accumulates, a gentle wear scenario can be achieved. Nevertheless, whether such glaze layer can be produced on the worn surface in time depends substantially on the sensitivity of the intrinsic structure in alloy matrix to tribochemical reactions. As for CCA, its wear resistance and thermal stability during high-temperature wear can be ameliorated by heterogeneous structural evolution. For example, coherent B2 nanoprecipitates and nano-layered pearlitic structure allow accelerated formation of protective glaze layers on worn TiMoNb CCA [] and Fe44.5Co25.4Ni24.4Ti5.7 CCA [] at 600 °C, respectively, while the Zener’s pinning effect associated with the (hetero-)interfaces can effectively suppress grain coarsening caused by sliding and heating.
